listeningScripts.title: Internet Service Outage
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, my internet's been down for three hours now and I need it for work. Support Agent: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me pull up your account. Can I have your account number? Customer: It's 4472-89156. I'm working from home and have a client call in twenty minutes. Agent: Got it. I see you're in the downtown Toronto area. We have a known outage affecting that postal code from a fiber cut about two hours ago. Our repair team is already on site. Customer: When will it be fixed? Agent: Based on the damage, they estimate two to three more hours. So around 4:30 PM at the latest. Customer: That's too late for my meeting. Can you give me a credit or something? Agent: Absolutely. Since this outage is on our end, I'll apply a $25 credit to your next bill automatically. That'll go through within 24 hours. Customer: What about my current bill? Do I get anything for today's service loss? Agent: Yes, we credit one day of service charges, which is about $3.50 for today. Combined with the $25 credit, that's $28.50 total compensation. Is there anything else I can help with? Customer: No, that's fair. Thank you.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Lunch Break
listeningScripts.text: Marcus: Hey, want to grab lunch together? Jessica: Sure, where are you thinking? Marcus: There's that new sushi place across the street. I've heard good things about it. Jessica: I'm not really in the mood for sushi. How about the Thai place on the corner? Marcus: That works too. I haven't tried that one yet. Jessica: They have great pad thai. We should go soon though, it gets busy after noon. Marcus: Good point. How about right now? Jessica: Perfect. I'll grab my wallet. Marcus: Do you think they have vegetarian options? Jessica: Definitely. They have a whole vegetarian section on the menu. Marcus: Great. Shall we? Jessica: Let's go. See you in five minutes downstairs.

listeningScripts.title: Museum Audio Guide: Canadian Art
listeningScripts.text: Welcome to the Canadian Art gallery. I'm your audio guide for this exhibition. Today, we're exploring paintings and sculptures created by Canadian artists from the 1920s to 1960s. We'll start with the Group of Seven landscape paintings in Room 102. These artists revolutionized how Canadians saw their own wilderness, particularly the forests and lakes of Ontario. The paintings you see here depict rugged landscapes using bold colors and dynamic brushstrokes. In Room 104, we have Emily Carr's totem pole paintings from British Columbia. Carr spent much of her career documenting Indigenous art and the Pacific Northwest landscape. Her work emphasizes the spiritual connection between people and nature. Moving to Room 106, you'll find abstract works by Borduas and Riopelle from the 1950s. These Montreal-based artists were part of the Automatiste movement, which rejected traditional artistic rules. Finally, in Room 108, we showcase sculpture by Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth, who visited Canada in the 1950s. Their organic forms were inspired by Canadian landscapes. This exhibition runs through September 30th. Thank you for visiting.

listeningScripts.title: Winnipeg Public Transit Modernization
listeningScripts.text: Winnipeg is modernizing its public transit system with a 450 million dollar investment over the next decade. The city has approved plans to purchase 300 new electric buses to replace aging diesel vehicles. The transition will eliminate approximately 8,500 tonnes of annual carbon emissions from the transportation sector. Current ridership stands at 89 million trips annually, and the city expects this to grow by 20 percent once new services launch. Construction of a new rapid transit corridor connecting downtown to the airport is set to begin next year. This corridor will reduce travel time from downtown to the airport from 45 minutes to just 22 minutes. The project includes the construction of 12 new transit stations along the corridor. Free transit passes will be offered to seniors and students to encourage ridership. Overall, the modernization is expected to create 1,100 permanent jobs in operations and maintenance. Winnipeg Transit has committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2040.

listeningScripts.title: Remote Work Policy Debate
listeningScripts.text:
Manager Sarah: I've been thinking about our remote work policy, and honestly, I think we need to bring people back to the office at least three days a week. When I worked from home during the pandemic, I felt disconnected from my team, and I worry about newer staff missing out on mentorship opportunities. Plus, collaboration seems to happen more naturally when people are in the same space.

Employee James: I completely understand your point, Sarah, but I've actually found the opposite to be true. Since working remotely, my productivity has increased by about 40 percent because I have fewer interruptions. I can focus better on complex projects. And I'm still collaborating regularly with my colleagues through video calls and shared documents. Honestly, three days in the office feels like a step backward for many of us who have adapted well to remote work.

HR Director Tom: Both of you raise valid concerns. The data we've collected shows mixed results. Some teams are more productive working remotely, while others struggle with communication and onboarding new hires. I think the solution isn't one-size-fits-all. Different departments might need different policies. Customer service teams probably need more in-person interaction, while our software developers seem to work just fine remotely. We should consider a hybrid approach that gives managers flexibility based on their specific team's needs.

listeningScripts.title: Algorithmic Bias in Hiring Systems
listeningScripts.text: Algorithmic bias in hiring is a serious problem that companies are using as a shortcut without taking responsibility for the consequences. Many organizations now use AI systems to screen resumes, assess candidate fit, and predict job performance. These systems seem objective—they're just mathematics, right? Wrong. These algorithms are trained on historical data, which includes decades of human bias. If women were historically excluded from leadership positions, the algorithm learns that pattern and replicates it. If certain demographics were underrepresented in technical roles, the algorithm reinforces that exclusion. Studies have documented this repeatedly. Amazon famously scrapped their hiring algorithm when they discovered it was discriminating against women. Google's recruiting algorithm showed bias against applicants from historically black colleges. These weren't intentional—that's precisely the problem. The systems' creators didn't set out to discriminate; they just trusted that math was unbiased, when in reality, data is never neutral. My argument is this: companies should not deploy algorithmic hiring systems without rigorous bias testing and external auditing. If you use an algorithm to screen candidates, you're making a business decision, and you're responsible for its outcomes. You can't hide behind the algorithm or claim you didn't know it was biased. Moreover, algorithms eliminate human judgment, nuance, and chance. They can't capture potential, resilience, or growth. Some of the most successful employees wouldn't have passed an algorithm. We need a return to more human-centered hiring while using algorithms cautiously and with oversight.
